stem: On the Start page, where does an analyst pick the file type or server to connect to?

options.text: The Data pane on the left of a worksheet
options.rationale: The Data pane lists the fields of a data source that already exists; it is not where connections start.

options.text: The Marks card on a worksheet
options.rationale: The Marks card controls how marks look; it has nothing to do with connecting to data.

options.text: The Connect pane on the left
options.rationale: It lists the connectors for files and servers, with More for the full list.

options.text: The Extract Data dialog on the Data Source page
options.rationale: That dialog sets options for an extract of a source you have already connected to.

explanation: The Connect pane on the Start page lists the connectors: files such as Microsoft Excel and Text file, and servers for databases and cloud services. After you pick one, Tableau opens the Data Source page.

stem: Driftlight's sessions live in a busy production database. Which kind of connector does the analyst choose to reach it?

options.text: A server connector for the database
options.rationale: Databases and cloud services are listed under servers in the Connect pane.

options.text: A file connector such as Text file
options.rationale: File connectors read a local or shared file, not a database server.

options.text: The Extract Data dialog
options.rationale: That dialog configures an extract; it is not a connector.

options.text: The Data menu's Refresh command
options.rationale: Refresh updates an existing extract; it does not create a connection.

explanation: The Connect pane splits connectors into files (Microsoft Excel, Text file and others) and servers (databases and cloud services). A production database is reached through a server connector.

stem: An analyst connects to a table, drags it to the canvas and opens a sheet without touching the setting in the upper-right corner of the Data Source page. What kind of data source is it?

options.text: An extract with all rows
options.rationale: An extract is only created when Extract is selected and the settings are saved.

options.text: An extract with a sample of rows
options.rationale: Sampling is a Number of Rows option of the Extract Data dialog, which was never opened.

options.text: A saved .tdsx data source
options.rationale: A .tdsx is only created by saving the data source, which did not happen here.

options.text: A live connection
options.rationale: Unless Extract is selected, the source stays live and each view queries it directly.

explanation: In the upper-right corner of the Data Source page you can select Extract. If you don't, the data source stays a live connection and every view queries the source.

stem: A manager changes a filter on a dashboard that uses a live connection. What does Tableau do?

options.text: It reads the rows from a local .hyper file
options.rationale: A .hyper file exists only when an extract has been created.

options.text: It sends a new query to the original data source
options.rationale: With a live connection, every interaction is answered by the source.

options.text: It keeps showing the old rows until the next refresh
options.rationale: Refreshing applies to extracts; a live connection has no snapshot to refresh.

options.text: It rebuilds the data source as an extract first
options.rationale: Tableau never converts a live connection to an extract on its own.

explanation: A live connection queries the original database or file whenever the view needs data, so the speed and the freshness are those of the source.

stem: An analyst needs a connector that is not shown in the Connect pane. What should they click to see the full list?

options.text: More
options.rationale: The More link expands the Connect pane to every available connector.

options.text: Add, next to the Connections heading
options.rationale: Add attaches a second connection inside a data source that already exists.

options.text: Extract, in the upper-right corner
options.rationale: That switches an existing connection to an extract.

options.text: Add to Saved Data Sources
options.rationale: That saves an existing data source as a file.

explanation: The Connect pane shows the most common connectors. Clicking More opens the complete list of files and servers.

stem: After connecting to a file, what happens on the Data Source page before the analyst starts building a view?

options.text: Tableau automatically builds a dashboard from the first table
options.rationale: Tableau does not build views for you; the analyst builds them on a sheet.

options.text: They must create an extract before any sheet can open
options.rationale: An extract is optional; without it the connection stays live.

options.text: They drag tables to the canvas and check the preview grid
options.rationale: Then they click a sheet tab to start building.

options.text: They must save the source as a .tds file
options.rationale: Saving a data source is optional and separate from connecting.

explanation: Connecting opens the Data Source page, where you drag tables to the canvas and inspect the preview grid. Clicking a sheet tab then lets you build.

stem: Which description of a live connection is accurate?

options.text: Tableau copies all rows into a .hyper file when you connect
options.rationale: That describes an extract, not a live connection.

options.text: Tableau stores the data inside the .tds file
options.rationale: A .tds never contains data, only connection details and metadata.

options.text: Tableau works only while the source is offline
options.rationale: A live connection needs the source to be reachable.

options.text: Tableau queries the original database or file each time it needs data
options.rationale: The data stays where it is.

explanation: A live connection sends queries to the source. Nothing is copied, which is why it always shows current data but depends on the source being available.

stem: Which two connectors are file connectors in the Connect pane? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: A production database server
options.rationale: Databases are listed under servers.

options.text: Microsoft Excel
options.rationale: Excel is one of the file connectors.

options.text: A cloud service
options.rationale: Cloud services are listed under servers.

options.text: Text file
options.rationale: Text file, such as a CSV, is a file connector.

options.text: The Extract Data dialog
options.rationale: That is a dialog for extract settings, not a connector.

explanation: Files such as Microsoft Excel and Text file are one group of connectors. Servers (databases and cloud services) are the other.

stem: Which two actions are possible on the Data Source page of a new live connection? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Drag tables to the canvas
options.rationale: Tables are added to the canvas from the left pane.

options.text: Run Extract > Refresh on the extract
options.rationale: There is no extract yet, so there is nothing to refresh.

options.text: Check the data in the preview grid
options.rationale: The grid shows the rows of the tables you added.

options.text: Build a bar chart directly on the canvas
options.rationale: The canvas holds tables and their relationships; charts are built on a worksheet.

options.text: Remove the extract with Extract > Remove
options.rationale: A live connection has no extract to remove.

explanation: The Data Source page is where you shape the connection: add tables to the canvas and check the preview grid. Extract commands apply only after an extract exists.

stem: Which two statements describe a live connection? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Views show what the source holds right now
options.rationale: Each query runs against the original data.

options.text: The data is saved in a .hyper file
options.rationale: That describes an extract.

options.text: Query speed depends on the source system
options.rationale: Tableau waits for the database or file to answer.

options.text: New rows appear only after Extract > Refresh
options.rationale: Refresh applies to extracts.

options.text: The data works offline once the workbook is saved
options.rationale: A live connection needs the source to be reachable.

explanation: Because a live connection queries the original data, it is always current and as fast as the source. Snapshots, refreshes and offline use belong to extracts.

stem: An analyst creates a live connection to a text file and starts building. Which three steps are part of that process? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Pick Text file in the Connect pane
options.rationale: The connector is the first choice.

options.text: Select Extract and click Save Settings
options.rationale: That creates an extract, not a live connection.

options.text: Point Tableau at the file
options.rationale: The file is chosen after the connector.

options.text: Right-click the source and choose Add to Saved Data Sources
options.rationale: That saves the source as a .tds or .tdsx; it is not needed to connect.

options.text: Click a sheet tab after dragging a table to the canvas
options.rationale: That starts the analysis.

options.text: Run Extract > Refresh
options.rationale: There is no extract to refresh.

explanation: Choose the connector, point it at the file, add a table and open a sheet. Extracts and saved data sources are optional extra steps.

stem: An analyst must keep working on a Driftlight workbook during a flight with no internet. Which data source type allows that?

options.text: A live connection to the production database
options.rationale: A live connection needs the source to be reachable.

options.text: An extract
options.rationale: Extracts allow for offline access to data.

options.text: A live connection to a reporting table
options.rationale: It is still a live connection and needs the server.

options.text: A cross-database join of two live connections
options.rationale: Both connections still query their sources live.

explanation: An extract is a local copy in a .hyper file, so views can be built without reaching the original source. A live connection cannot work if the source is unreachable.

stem: The operations room needs a tile that shows today's sign-ups the moment they are stored in a reporting table. What should the data source be?

options.text: An extract refreshed every night
options.rationale: A nightly snapshot is up to a day old.

options.text: An extract with an incremental refresh
options.rationale: It still shows new rows only after a refresh runs.

options.text: A .tds file with the data stored inside
options.rationale: A .tds contains no data at all.

options.text: A live connection
options.rationale: Each query returns the rows the table holds now.

explanation: When people need up-to-the-minute data and the source can answer fast enough, a live connection is the right choice. An extract is only as current as its last refresh.

stem: The production database is slow during the day and every dashboard click adds to the load. Data that is one day old is fine. What is the best option?

options.text: Use an extract and refresh it every night
options.rationale: Queries hit the extract, sparing the database.

options.text: Keep the live connection and add more filters
options.rationale: The database is still queried on every click.

options.text: Save the live connection as a .tds file
options.rationale: A .tds stores no data, so queries still go to the database.

options.text: Connect to the same table twice
options.rationale: Both connections would query the busy database.

explanation: Extracts prevent resource drains on database systems and usually give faster views. A nightly refresh keeps the snapshot fresh enough for this need.

stem: How does the data in an extract change after it is created?

options.text: Continuously, as the original source changes
options.rationale: That is how a live connection behaves.

options.text: Whenever the workbook is opened
options.rationale: Opening the workbook does not update the snapshot.

options.text: Only when the extract is refreshed
options.rationale: It is a snapshot until then.

options.text: Whenever someone filters a view
options.rationale: Filters change what is shown, not what the extract contains.

explanation: An extract is a copy saved separately from the original data, so it differs from the source until you refresh it.

stem: What does an extract use to store its data?

options.text: A .tds file
options.rationale: A .tds holds connection details and metadata but no data.

options.text: A .hyper file
options.rationale: The extract is a subset of the data saved separately from the original.

options.text: A .twb file
options.rationale: A .twb workbook holds worksheets and dashboards but no data.

options.text: A .twbx file
options.rationale: A .twbx packages a workbook with local files; it is not the extract format.

explanation: An extract is saved as a .hyper file. Workbook and data source files (.twb, .twbx, .tds, .tdsx) are different things, though packaged ones can contain an extract.

stem: The database behind a data source does not support a function the analyst wants to use in a calculation. Which approach can help?

options.text: Keep the live connection and refresh it
options.rationale: Live connections have nothing to refresh, and they depend on the source's own functions.

options.text: Save the data source as a .tds
options.rationale: A .tds saves metadata, not new functions.

options.text: Use an extract
options.rationale: Extracts can give access to functions the source does not support.

options.text: Add a second connection to the same database
options.rationale: The second connection is still limited by that database.

explanation: With a live connection you use the source's own functions. An extract can give access to functions the source doesn't support.

stem: Which feature is an advantage of a live connection over an extract?

options.text: It allows offline access
options.rationale: Offline access is an advantage of extracts.

options.text: It lets you keep only the top N rows
options.rationale: Limiting rows is an extract setting.

options.text: It reduces the load on the database
options.rationale: Live connections query the database on every interaction.

options.text: It uses the source's own functions and collation
options.rationale: The query is answered by the source itself.

explanation: A live connection hands the work to the source, so its own functions and collation apply. Offline access and lower load come with extracts.

stem: A Driftlight extract was fully refreshed at midnight. A new session row is stored in the database at 9 a.m. When does it show up in views on the extract?

options.text: After the next refresh of the extract
options.rationale: The extract is a snapshot until refreshed.

options.text: Immediately, because Tableau checks the database
options.rationale: That would be a live connection.

options.text: When a different analyst opens the workbook
options.rationale: Opening a workbook does not refresh the extract.

options.text: When the sheet tab is clicked again
options.rationale: Switching sheets redraws views from the same snapshot.

explanation: Views on an extract query the .hyper file, so changes in the original source appear only after the extract is refreshed.

stem: Which two situations favour an extract over a live connection? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The analyst must work offline
options.rationale: Extracts allow offline access.

options.text: Dashboards must show data from the last minute
options.rationale: Only a live connection gives up-to-the-minute data.

options.text: The database is busy and should not be queried on every click
options.rationale: Queries go to the extract instead.

options.text: The analyst needs the source's own collation
options.rationale: That is a reason to stay live.

options.text: The data may never be copied from the source
options.rationale: An extract is a copy of the data.

explanation: Extracts help with offline work, speed and load on the source. A live connection is better for current data and the source's own features.

stem: Which two reasons support choosing a live connection? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The data must be as current as the source
options.rationale: Each query returns the present state.

options.text: The workbook must work without network access
options.rationale: That needs an extract.

options.text: The source is fast enough to answer interactively
options.rationale: Speed is that of the source, so a fast source suits live use.

options.text: The source is slow and busy
options.rationale: That points to an extract.

options.text: A packaged copy of the data must travel with the workbook
options.rationale: Packaging data is done with extracts or packaged files.

explanation: Choose live when people need up-to-the-minute data and the database answers fast enough. Slow or busy sources and offline needs point to an extract.

stem: Which three statements about extracts compared with live connections are correct? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: An extract is stored in a .hyper file
options.rationale: It is saved separately from the original data.

options.text: Views on an extract can perform better than views on the original data
options.rationale: This is the performance benefit of extracts.

options.text: An extract can be refreshed on demand
options.rationale: Refresh updates it from the source.

options.text: A live connection keeps working with no access to its source
options.rationale: A live connection needs the source.

options.text: An extract updates itself each time a view is drawn
options.rationale: It changes only when refreshed.

options.text: A live connection stores a snapshot in a .hyper file
options.rationale: Snapshots belong to extracts.

explanation: An extract is a .hyper snapshot that is usually faster and can be refreshed when you choose. A live connection has no local copy.

stem: Where does an analyst begin creating an extract in Tableau Desktop?

options.text: Right-click the data source and choose Add to Saved Data Sources
options.rationale: That saves a .tds or .tdsx; it does not create an extract.

options.text: Click Add next to the Connections heading
options.rationale: That adds another connection to the data source.

options.text: Select Extract in the upper-right corner of the Data Source page, then click Edit
options.rationale: This opens the Extract Data dialog.

options.text: Choose Data > Extract > Refresh
options.rationale: Refresh updates an existing extract; it cannot create one.

explanation: On the Data Source page, select Extract in the upper-right corner and click Edit to open the Extract Data dialog and choose its settings.

stem: An analyst wants the extract to contain only Driftlight sessions from 2025. Which setting in the Extract Data dialog does this?

options.text: Filters
options.rationale: Filters keep only the rows you need.

options.text: Roll up dates to Year
options.rationale: That aggregates dates to a level such as month; it does not select a year.

options.text: Number of Rows set to Sample
options.rationale: A sample keeps rows chosen at random, not those of a year.

options.text: Hide All Unused Fields
options.rationale: That removes unused fields, not rows.

explanation: An extract filter works on the data before any view sees it, so rows that fail the filter are not in the extract at all.

stem: After choosing settings in the Extract Data dialog and clicking Save Settings, what starts the creation of the extract?

options.text: Choosing Data > Extract > Refresh
options.rationale: Refresh is for updating an extract that already exists.

options.text: Closing and reopening Tableau Desktop
options.rationale: Nothing is built on restart.

options.text: Selecting Live in the upper-right corner
options.rationale: That would switch the data source back to a live connection.

options.text: Clicking a sheet tab
options.rationale: Tableau builds the extract when the analyst opens a sheet.

explanation: Save Settings only stores the extract options. Clicking a sheet tab begins building the extract.

stem: An analyst hid several unneeded fields in the Data pane and wants them left out of the extract. Which option should be selected in the Extract Data dialog?

options.text: Aggregate data for visible dimensions
options.rationale: That stores pre-aggregated rows instead of every record; it is not about fields.

options.text: Hide All Unused Fields
options.rationale: Hidden fields are then left out of the extract.

options.text: Incremental refresh
options.rationale: That is a refresh method and says nothing about fields.

options.text: Physical Tables
options.rationale: That chooses how the extract stores tables, not which fields.

explanation: Hide All Unused Fields leaves hidden fields out of the extract, which makes the file smaller.

stem: Which two settings can an analyst choose in the Extract Data dialog? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Filters
options.rationale: They limit the rows kept in the extract.

options.text: Add to Saved Data Sources
options.rationale: This is a command on the data source's right-click menu.

options.text: Number of Rows: All rows, Top, or Sample
options.rationale: It limits how many rows are extracted.

options.text: Extract > History
options.rationale: That is a command on the Data menu.

options.text: Add a connection
options.rationale: Connections are added from the Connections pane.

explanation: The Extract Data dialog holds the options for the extract itself, such as filters and the number of rows. Saving sources and viewing history are separate commands.
